## A melody that has to accompany itself

You've sung one. *Frère Jacques*, *Row, Row, Row Your Boat*, *London's
Burning*: a *canon* is a melody that works as its own accompaniment, because a
second voice enters with the same tune after a delay and the two halves happen
to fit. Nothing gets added. One tune, played against a shifted copy of itself.

That constraint lands entirely on the melody. In every arrangement so far you
picked a bass, or a counter-line, or a chord, and you could change it when it
didn't work. A canon takes that away. Bar 3 of the subject has to make a
sensible vertical interval with bar 1, because bar 1 is what will be sounding
underneath it, and your only two controls are how long you wait and how far you
transpose.

Two parameters, then. Entry delay decides *which* positions in the subject meet
each other. Transposition decides what interval each of those meetings produces.
Pick a pair at random and you'll get repeated seconds, or every voice crammed
into one register, or a cadence that arrives while another voice is mid-phrase.
That result is evidence, not failure. It shows that a canonic subject carries
its own accompaniment inside it, and that delay alone won't manufacture
counterpoint from a melody that has none.

Each voice runs in its own thread. One array holds the subject and nobody edits
it. Entry time, transposition, synth and amplitude belong to the description of
a voice, not to the melody being imitated.

## Three entries, one bar apart

The subject below runs four beats: C up to G, then back down to C. Three voices
enter four beats apart, the third an octave lower, and each repeats the subject
sixteen times. The subject is four beats long and the entries are four beats
apart. Once all three voices are in, what do you expect them to be doing?

```{.ruby audio=""}
use_bpm 96

subject = [
  {note: 60, start: 0.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 64, start: 0.5, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 67, start: 1.0, duration: 1.0},
  {note: 65, start: 2.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 64, start: 2.5, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 62, start: 3.0, duration: 0.5},
  {note: 60, start: 3.5, duration: 0.5}
]

define :play_events do |events, transpose_by, amp|
  cursor = 0.0
  events.each do |event|
    sleep event[:start] - cursor
    play event[:note] + transpose_by,
      release: event[:duration] * 0.8,
      amp: amp
    cursor = event[:start]
  end
  sleep events.last[:duration]
end

entries = [
  {delay: 0, transpose: 0, synth: :piano, amp: 0.85},
  {delay: 4, transpose: 0, synth: :pluck, amp: 0.65},
  {delay: 8, transpose: -12, synth: :hollow, amp: 0.5}
]

entries.each do |entry|
  in_thread do
    sleep entry[:delay]
    use_synth entry[:synth]
    16.times { play_events subject, entry[:transpose], entry[:amp] }
  end
end
```

Sixteen repetitions at 96 bpm means the whole thing runs about three quarters of
a minute, and the last voice finishes five seconds after the first. Nothing has
hung. Stop it early once you've heard what you need.

Here's what you'll actually hear, and it's worth naming plainly, because it
isn't a canon. The subject is four beats long and the delay is four beats, so
the follower's first note lands exactly on the leader's second repetition. From
that point on all three voices play the same pitches at the same moments, one of
them an octave down. Staggered entrances, then a unison doubling. That's the
degenerate case, and it's the reference you're about to move away from.

## Move the delay, then move the transposition

1. Change the second delay from `4` to `2`. Now the follower enters halfway
   through the leader's subject and stays there. This is where the canon
   actually starts. Work out which note pairs are sounding together before you
   run it, then check yourself against the log.
2. Restore the delay and set the second transposition to `7`, entering a fifth
   higher. Some intervals open out in pitch-class terms while the follower moves
   into closer competition with the leader's register. Listen for harmonic fit
   and for your own ability to follow two contours, separately.
3. Change the subject's fourth note from `65` to `66`. Every voice reads the
   same array, so that F-sharp appears three times over, at three different
   points in the cycle. Mark every unstable meeting it creates. Then decide
   whether the note or the entry plan is what needs revising.

## Delay chooses a whole map of intervals

Take variation 1 seriously for a moment, because the arithmetic is small enough
to do by hand. With a two-beat delay, the follower is the leader shifted forward
two beats, so at any moment the follower sounds whatever the leader sounded two
beats earlier. Line the four beats up:

| Beat | Leader | Follower | Interval |
|------|--------|----------|----------|
| 0.0  | C      | F        | fourth   |
| 0.5  | E      | E        | unison   |
| 1.0  | G      | D        | fourth   |
| 1.5  | G      | C        | fifth    |
| 2.0  | F      | C        | fourth   |
| 2.5  | E      | E        | unison   |
| 3.0  | D      | G        | fourth   |
| 3.5  | C      | G        | fifth    |

Fourths, fifths and unisons, all the way through. That's an open, hollow sound,
closer to medieval organum than to anything with a third in it. Delay picked
that entire column for you. Change it to four beats and every row collapses to a
unison; change it to one beat and you'd get a different column again, this time
containing seconds. So a single number selects a whole map of vertical
relationships, and you can compute the map before you hear it.

Consonance is only the first test that map has to pass. A long run of stable
thirds sounds motionless. Intervals that are individually agreeable can still
drag both voices toward cadences at unhelpful moments. What you want is a
subject with a recognisable contour, rhythmic life in each voice, and overlaps
that imply changing harmony across the cycle.

Transposition then shifts every interval in the map at once. Enter at a fifth
and several scale relationships survive while another tonic becomes plausible.
Enter at an octave and pitch classes stay identical while register clears up.
Test delay first, transposition second. When a collision appears, that order
tells you which parameter caused it.

## Where the subject stops and the voice begins

The subject array is immutable score data. Nothing in the program writes to it,
which is what makes the word *imitation* honest: all three voices are provably
reading the same melody. The entry records carry delay, transposition, synth and
amplitude, because those describe how one particular voice presents the subject.
You've seen this division before, between musical form and rendering. One object
stays identifiable while several calls place it in different contexts.

Absolute `:start` values keep the subject compatible with `play_events` from the
transcription lessons, and with the capstones ahead. Each repetition resets its
local cursor at the subject boundary, so a canon is just the same renderer
called from three threads with three offsets. Entry delay lives outside the
subject on purpose. It belongs to the imitating voice, and putting it inside
would mean each voice needed its own edited copy of the melody, which is exactly
the thing a canon is not.

## Write a subject that survives its own echo

Write an eight-beat subject and use it, unchanged, in a three-voice canon
running at least sixteen bars. Compare delays of two, four and eight beats with
all voices at unison. Once you've chosen a delay, compare unison, octave and
fifth transpositions against it. Keep every entry specification separately
inspectable.

Then find the three overlaps where the vertical relationship is most exposed and
name the implied chord or interval at each one in a comment. Your final choice
should come out of those comparisons. If you find yourself editing a separate
copy of the subject for one of the voices, stop: you've stopped writing a canon
and started writing three parts.
